abstract: Detecting vessels in noisy underwater recordings requires useful sound clues and efficient computation. We contribute a reproducible framework that links sound representation, tests of AI-generated evidence and processing cost. First, it compares descriptions of the same sound, including its tones and how they change over time. Second, it compares detector responses to two edits: replacing a short sound segment with AI-generated background, and applying a control edit designed to cause similar disturbance. Tests with and without the generated-evidence score identify a stronger scoring configuration while keeping the remaining procedures unchanged. Third, it compares a language-model agent selecting tools from numerical detector summaries with fixed procedures, measuring detection scores and processing time. On recordings labelled using vessel tracking, a neural network using sound images (spectrograms) scored more strongly than the preselected comparison method, providing a tested reference detector. Fixed verification reproduced the agent's observed detection score with substantially less processing time, establishing a simpler alternative on this cohort. A separate network successfully detected known activity periods in synthetic scenes, providing a controlled test of activity timing. Numerical checks made signal-analysis reliability an explicit criterion for choosing representations. Together, these results provide reusable baselines, controlled checks of generated evidence and practical guidance for selecting detection methods and allocating computing resources.

changes.old: Underwater monitoring requires methods that extract useful clues from noisy sound while making efficient use of computing resources. We present a reproducible framework for comparing complementary descriptions of the same recording: its tones, their timing and changes across scales. The methodological contribution integrates generated background replacements, approximately matched control edits, tests with and without the verification score, recorded agent choices and measured processing costs. This controlled design makes the contribution of each added AI step assessable. A language-model agent selects tools from numerical detector summaries. On the studied recordings, labelled using vessel-tracking records, a neural network using sound images (spectrograms) achieved stronger detection scores than the preselected wavelet detector. A separate network established effective reference performance for constructed activity intervals in synthetic scenes. Fixed verification reproduced the agent's observed detection score with substantially less computation, identifying a practical opportunity to simplify orchestration. Score-removal tests identified a stronger scoring configuration while preserving tool use and calibration, and numerical checks clarified which signal-processing components were ready for primary evaluation. Real-data comparisons describe the evaluated cohort, with repeated vessels across days; synthetic results describe constructed activity. Together, these findings provide tested baselines and a reusable way to connect acoustic representation, verification design and computational demand, supporting more informed choices for underwater monitoring.

changes.new: Fourier spectra, spectrograms and wavelets expose different frequency and time structure in the same underwater waveform. We combine representation benchmarking, controlled verification and measured computing cost to guide detector design (Fig.~\ref{fig:1}). The language model receives numerical detector outputs; a separate convolutional neural network (CNN) processes spectrograms. Labels indicate vessel presence from automatic identification system (AIS) records.
changes.old: Fourier spectra, spectrograms and wavelets expose different frequency and time structure in the same underwater waveform. We combine representation benchmarking with controlled verification and measured computing cost to guide detection-system design (Fig.~\ref{fig:1}). The language-model controller receives numerical detector outputs; a separate CNN processes two-dimensional log-mel spectrograms. The real-data target is AIS-linked window presence.

changes.new: Comparison and verification workflow. Fourier, short-time Fourier transform (STFT) and wavelet views are primary. A bounded Hilbert--Huang transform (HHT) approximation explores decomposition into oscillating components. The agent chooses tools; numerical detectors score evidence.
changes.old: Implemented evidence and verification workflow. Fourier, STFT and wavelet measurements are primary. HHT is exploratory. The language model selects tools; the numeric head retains responsibility for calibrated predictions.
